How to use this course

This course is about the Abhidhamma (the higher teaching), the part of the Buddha’s teaching that explains what a person really is: not a lasting someone, but moments of mind and matter arising and falling away, one after another. It has twelve lessons. Each lesson explains one part of the Abhidhamma in plain words, and most lessons also tell a true story from the ancient texts.

Pāḷi words. The Buddha’s teaching was written down in a language called Pāḷi. You will meet Pāḷi words all through this course. Every time one appears, its English meaning sits right next to it in brackets, like this: citta (consciousness), rūpa (matter). You never have to remember a Pāḷi word to understand the page. But if you do remember a few, you will be able to read the ancient texts one day.

Saying the words. A line over a letter makes it long: ā sounds like the “a” in “father”, ī like the “ee” in “see”, ū like the “oo” in “moon”. A dot under a letter (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ) means you curl your tongue back a little. ñ sounds like the “ny” in “canyon”. ṃ sounds like “ng”. So paññā is said “pan-nyaa” and saṅkhāra is said “sang-khaa-ra”.

Numbers. The Abhidhamma counts things: 89 kinds of citta (consciousness), 52 cetasika (mental factors), 28 kinds of rūpa (matter), 31 planes of existence. Nobody has to learn the numbers by heart. They are there to show that the Abhidhamma leaves nothing vague.

Hard words. Some English words in this book are hard. The first time a hard word is met in a chapter it has a small number after it, like this: aeons⁵. Its meaning is given at the end of the chapter, under “Hard words in this chapter”, and all the hard words are listed together at the back, after the word list. In the web edition, tapping or clicking on the word shows its meaning.

Quizzes. After every two lessons there is a short quiz.

Where it comes from. The course follows a small book, An Introduction to the Abhidhamma, printed for free distribution by the Dhamma Study Group in Bangkok in 1980. It has two essays: Abhidhamma Notes by Jill Jordan and Richard Giles, which Lessons 1 to 10 follow, and Abhidhamma and Practice by Nina van Gorkom, which Lessons 11 and 12 follow. At the back the book has an appendix listing all the paramattha dhamma (absolute realities), and the lists in Lessons 3, 4 and 5 come from it. The stories of how the Abhidhamma was taught and handed down come from the ancient commentaries and chronicles: the Atthasālinī (The Expositor), the Dhammapada commentary and the Mahāvaṃsa (the Great Chronicle of Ceylon). A sentence in quotation marks is a quotation from the book or from the ancient texts in translation.

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  3

Introduction: what is the Abhidhamma?

“Better than a thousand useless words, is one useful word hearing which, one attains peace.” Dhammapada 100, as quoted at the front of the book this course follows.

The word. Abhidhamma is a word in Pāḷi, the language in which the Buddha’s teachings were recorded and handed down. Abhi means “higher” or “greater”. Dhamma means “reality1” or “truth”; the book says it “can be loosely translated as to mean ‘everything which is real’”. So Abhidhamma means “the higher truth” or “the higher teaching”. The three baskets. The Buddha’s teachings in Pāḷi are called the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets). The Abhidhamma is the third basket.

1 2 3

Vinaya Piṭaka Sutta Piṭaka Abhidhamma Piṭaka the Basket of Discipline the Basket of Discourses the Basket of the Higher Teaching

rules for monks and nuns discourses, stories and verses everything taken apart and named “It is the third of the three sections of the Pāḷi Canon (the collected teachings of the Buddha in the Pāḷi language).”

1. The Vinaya Piṭaka (the Basket of Discipline): the rules for the monks2 and nuns3 of the Saṅgha (the order). 2. The Sutta Piṭaka (the Basket of Discourses4): the discourses, stories and verses given by the Buddha and his disciples5. 3. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka (the Basket of the Higher Teaching): the book calls it “the philosophical6 and analytical7 summation8 of the teachings”. It takes everything apart and names every piece. The seven books. The Abhidhamma is a collection of seven books.

Dhammasaṅgaṇī Vibhaṅga Dhātukathā Puggalapaññatti Kathāvatthu Yamaka Paṭṭhāna enumeration treatises elements types of persons controversies pairs of questions conditions “The Abhidhamma consists of seven books.”

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  4

Page 4
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 5

Book What it is Dhammasaṅgaṇī the enumeration9 of all mental10 and material11 phenomena12 Vibhaṅga the book of treatises13 of all phenomena Dhātukathā the discussion of the groups, bases and elements14 of existence Puggalapaññatti the description of individual types of persons Kathāvatthu the discussion of points of controversy15 with schismatic16 sects Yamaka the book of pairs of questions the book of origination17, conditionality and dependence of all the phenomena of Paṭṭhāna existence

The seventh, the Paṭṭhāna (the book of conditions18), is the largest and the most important Abhidhamma work.

No persons, no places, no things. The books of the Abhidhamma “analyse in minute detail the mental states and material states that comprise what we call our life and what we call the world”. In all that detail there is no mention of persons, places or objects19. The book says why: “they do not exist in the ultimate20 sense”. A name like “Anna” or “Bangkok” or “table” is a label, useful for talking. What really exists is two sorts of thing: nāma (mind, that which experiences21) and rūpa (matter22, that which does not experience). What is called a person, a place or a thing is really “different types of mental and material phenomena occurring one after another with extreme rapidity23 and giving the appearance of a coherent and lasting whole”.

The chariot. The ancient teachers explained this with a chariot24. The book quotes the Visuddhimagga (the Path of Purity25), written by the great commentator26 Buddhaghosa:

“Just as the word ‘chariot’ is but a mode of expression for axle, wheels, chariot-body, pole and other constituent27 members, placed in a certain relation to each other, but when we come to examine the members one by one, we discover that in the absolute28 sense there is no chariot. And just as the word ‘house’ is but a mode of expression for wood and other constituents of a house, surrounding space in a certain relation, but in the absolute sense there is no house. And just as the word ‘fist’ is but a mode of expression for the fingers, the thumb, etc., in a certain relation, but when we come to examine the parts one by one we discover that in the absolute sense there is no fist; in exactly the same way the words ‘living being29’ and ‘ego30’ are but a mode of expression for the presence of the five attachment31 groups but when we come to examine the elements of being one by one, we discover that in the absolute sense there is no living being there to form a basis for such figments32 as ‘I am’ or ‘I’; in other words that in the absolute sense there is only mentality and materiality (nama and rupa).”

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  5

Page 5
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 6

pole axle body take it apart no chariot only parts in a certain relation “person”: only nāma and rūpa wheels “chariot” a name for the parts together “when we come to examine the members one by one, we discover that in the absolute sense there is no chariot”

The chariot picture is older than Buddhaghosa. In the Saṃyutta Nikāya (the Grouped Discourses) a nun called Vajirā is asked by Māra, the tempter, who made “this sentient33 being”. She answers in verse:

“This is just a pile of conditions, you won’t find a sentient being here. When the parts are assembled we use the word ‘chariot’. So too, when the aggregates34 are present ‘sentient being’ is the convention35 we use.”

Moments. The preface to the book puts it another way. “It is made clear that life exists as moments only. The past moments have gone, they cannot be made to come back. The future has not yet come, so it does not yet exist. The present moment is now and is all that really exists.” The moment of seeing is different from the moment of hearing; hearing is different from thinking about what is heard; “even the taste is not the same as the tasting”.

Good and bad. The Abhidhamma sorts all moments of consciousness36 into four kinds: kusala (good) moments, akusala (bad) moments, moments that are the result37 of past causes, and moments that are neither. Through this sorting, the book says, “one establishes also a moral38 and harmonious39 way to live so as to benefit oneself and others in the course of life”. And in the end, “through Abhidhamma one comes to understand reality as it is so that ignorance40 of the true nature of reality can be eliminated41 forever and there is no more cause for going on.”

What the lessons cover. Lesson 1 tells how the Abhidhamma was taught and handed down. Lesson 2 explains nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter) and the four paramattha dhamma (absolute realities). Lessons 3, 4 and 5 take citta (consciousness), cetasika (mental factors42) and rūpa (matter) one by one. Lesson 6 is about kamma (deeds43) and vipāka (result). Lesson 7 is about birth and death. Lesson 8 is about the four stages of enlightenment44. Lesson 9 is about the chain of conditions, the Four Noble Truths and the three marks. Lesson 10 asks what is happening right now. Lessons 11 and 12 follow the second essay in the

book, on what the Abhidhamma has to do with practice.

Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 8

Lesson 1: how the Abhidhamma came down to us

“The teachings of the Abhidhamma it is said were first taught to the Buddha’s mother and residents of some of the heavenly realms”

Taught in heaven. The book says that the teachings of the Abhidhamma “were first taught to the Buddha’s mother and residents of some of the heavenly realms1 during a period of three months in the seventh year after the Buddha’s enlightenment2“. The ancient commentary3 on the first book of the Abhidhamma, the Atthasālinī (The Expositor), tells the story in full.

The Buddha’s mother, Queen Māyā, had died seven days after he was born, and was reborn4 as a deva (heavenly being5) in Tusita (the heaven of the contented). In the seventh year after his enlightenment the Buddha went up to Tāvatiṃsa (the heaven of the Thirty-three), ruled by Sakka (the king of the heavenly beings). He sat on Sakka’s stone seat at the foot of the great coral tree. The devas (heavenly beings) of ten thousand world systems came to listen, and his mother came down from Tusita (the heaven of the contented) to sit at their head. There, for the three months of the rainy season, day and night without a break, the Buddha taught the Abhidhamma.

The created Buddha. A human body cannot go three months without food. So each day, the commentary says, the Buddha created an image of himself, a nimmita (created) Buddha, which went on teaching exactly as he would, while he himself went down to the lake Anotatta in the Himalayas to wash, and to the northern land of Uttarakuru for alms6. Every day his chief disciple7 Sāriputta came to wait on him by the lake, and the Buddha told him the method of what had been taught in heaven that day: “so much has been taught”.

Sāriputta’s five hundred pupils. Sāriputta taught it to his five hundred pupils, “neither too briefly nor too elaborately”. Long before, in the time of the Buddha Kassapa, those five hundred had been bats, hanging in a cave where two learned monks8 used to recite9 the Abhidhamma. The bats could not understand a word, but they liked the sound of the voices, and they died with that sound in mind. For that they were

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  8

Page 8
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 9

reborn as devas (heavenly beings), and in the time of our Buddha as human beings, who became monks under Sāriputta. The book says: “Sariputta in turn taught the Abhidhamma to the monks under his instruction, whose role it was to memorise and master it. In this way the seven books of the Abhidhamma have come down to us intact10.”

the Buddha 500 monks Third Council written down Tāvatiṃsa heaven memorised it Pāṭaliputta on palm leaves three months King Asoka Sri Lanka

Sāriputta First Council Mahinda at lake Anotatta Rājagaha to Sri Lanka each day 500 arahants

“In this way the seven books of the Abhidhamma have come down to us intact.”

The descent from heaven. When the three months were over, the Buddha came down to the human world at the city of Saṅkassa. The Dhammapada commentary tells that Sakka had three staircases made from the top of Mount Sineru, the mountain at the centre of the world, down to the city gate: one of gold for the devas (heavenly beings), one of silver for the Brahmās (the highest heavenly beings), and one of jewels in the middle for the Buddha.

Why heaven? A deva (heavenly being) can sit for three months without eating or sleeping. The Abhidhamma is long, and its sections depend on one another, so it has to be taught without a break.

The First Council. Three months after the Buddha passed away, five hundred arahants (fully enlightened disciples) met at Rājagaha, led by the Elder Mahākassapa, and recited the whole teaching together so that it would be remembered exactly. The Elder Upāli recited the Vinaya (the discipline) and the Elder Ānanda the Suttas (the discourses11). The Atthasālinī (The Expositor) says the Abhidhamma was recited at that same council12. A saṅgīti (a council) is a chanting together.

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  9

Page 9
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 10

“Previous to this the entire Pāḷi Canon had been committed to memory in verse form by groups of monks”

Carried in memory. For a long time nothing was written down. The book says the entire Pāḷi canon13 “had been committed to memory in verse form by groups of monks”. Each group kept one part. A boy who became a novice14 learned his part from his teacher word by word, and taught it to his own pupils when he was old.

The Second and Third Councils. A hundred years after the Buddha, seven hundred arahants (fully enlightened disciples) met at Vesālī and recited the teaching again. Then, in the reign15 of King Asoka, who ruled nearly the whole of India, a thousand arahants (fully enlightened disciples) met at the capital, Pāṭaliputta, under the Elder Moggaliputta Tissa. At that council the Elder set out the fifth book of the Abhidhamma, the Kathāvatthu (Points of Controversy16), answering wrong views17 that had crept in among the monks. He followed a mātikā (a table of headings) that the Buddha himself had laid down for the purpose.

Mahinda goes to Sri Lanka. After the Third Council, King Asoka’s son, the Elder Mahinda, was sent to the island of Sri Lanka (Ceylon). The Mahāvaṃsa (the Great Chronicle18 of Ceylon) tells how he arrived. The king of the island, Devānampiyatissa, had gone hunting on the Missaka mountain. A deva (heavenly being), wanting the king to meet the monks, took the form of a stag19 and let itself be seen in a thicket20. The king chased it up the mountain, and the stag led him to the Elder, who was waiting there with his companions. “Come hither21, Tissa,” said the Elder. The king was alarmed that a stranger called him by name. The Elder said: “Samanas are we, O great king, disciples of the King of Truth. From compassion22 toward thee23 are we come hither from Jambudipa.”

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  10

Page 10
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 11

“Samanas are we, O great king, disciples of the King of Truth.”

Before he taught, Mahinda wanted to know whether the king was quick enough to follow. So he asked him about a mango tree standing nearby.

“What name does this tree bear, O king?” “This tree is called a mango.” “Is there yet another mango beside this?” “There are many mango-trees.” “And are there yet other trees besides this mango and the other mangoes?” “There are many trees, sir; but those are trees that are not mangoes.” “And are there, beside the other mangoes and those trees which are not mangoes, yet other trees?” “There is this mango-tree, sir.” “Thou hast a shrewd24 wit25, O ruler of men!”

“When he had known that he was a keen-witted man,” the chronicle says, “the wise thera26 preached to the monarch” a discourse of the Buddha, the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta (the Shorter Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint). From that time Sri Lanka became the home of the Tipiṭaka (the Three Baskets). Mahinda brought the Abhidhamma with the rest, and the commentaries too.

Written down. More than four hundred years after the Buddha, in the reign of King Vaṭṭagāmaṇī Abhaya, the island suffered war and famine27, and the monks feared that the teaching might be lost if the reciters died. So they met and wrote the whole of it on palm leaves. The Mahāvaṃsa (the Great Chronicle of Ceylon) says: “The text of the three pitakas and the atthakatha thereon did the most wise bhikkhus hand down in former times orally, but since they saw that the people were falling away28 (from religion) the bhikkhus came together, and in order that the true doctrine might endure29, they wrote them down in

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  11

Page 11
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 12

books.” The aṭṭhakathā (commentaries) are the ancient explanations of the texts. The book says that from the Third Council onwards the seven books “were considered completed and not subject to alteration30 in any way”, and that “unaltered copies of the entire Canon have existed in Sri Lanka until the present day”.

“in order that the true doctrine might endure, they wrote them down in books.”

Why it matters. The ancient texts say the seven books are the Buddha’s own teaching, given in heaven, handed to Sāriputta, recited by the arahants (fully enlightened disciples) at the councils, carried in memory for four centuries, and written down in Sri Lanka. Every lesson in this course is a small piece of what was taught under the coral tree.

Lesson 2: the two kinds of reality

“Seeing is not hearing. They do not occur together, they occur at different moments”

Nāma and rūpa. The book says: “There are two kinds of absolute1 realities2 (paramattha dhammas). They are mental3 phenomena4 (nama) and physical or material5 phenomena (rupa). Nama experiences6 something. Rupa does not experience anything.” That is the whole difference. Nāma (mind) knows; rūpa (matter7) is known and knows nothing.

Seeing. Seeing is a kind of nāma (mind): it experiences its object8, colour, which the book calls “visible data”. Colour is a kind of rūpa (matter). It does not experience anything. The same goes for all five senses. Seeing, hearing, tasting, touching and smelling each experience an object. The objects, colour, sound, flavour, hardness and smell, are rūpa (matter), and experience nothing.

nāma rūpa mind: it experiences something matter: it experiences nothing experiences seeing colour experiences hearing sound experiences smelling smell experiences tasting flavour experiences touching hardness

“Nama experiences something. Rupa does not experience anything.”

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  14

Page 14
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 15

So seeing and what is seen are not the same thing. One knows; the other is known. A child looking at a flower may think that the flower and the seeing are one thing. The Abhidhamma takes them apart: there is colour, which is rūpa (matter), and there is seeing, which is nāma (mind).

Different moments. Each type of nāma (mind) and each type of rūpa (matter) is different from every other. Seeing is not hearing. The book says: “They do not occur together, they occur at different moments, although we are under the impression that they do occur together.” At the table there seems to be a whole scene at once: the sight of the food, the sound of talking, the taste, the smell, the hardness of the spoon. In reality these are five different experiences, each at its own moment, following one another so fast that they seem to be one.

The six doors. The ancient texts speak of six dvāra (doors) through which objects are experienced. Five are the senses; the sixth is the mind.

The citta (consciousness9) that experiences it Door Object eye colour seeing ear sound hearing nose smell smelling tongue flavour tasting body hardness, heat, motion experiencing through the body mind nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter), the consciousness that experiences through the mindand concepts10 door, such as thinking

Each of the five sense-door consciousnesses takes its own object and no other: seeing experiences only colour, hearing only sound. The consciousness at the mind-door can experience nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter) of every kind, and concepts as well. Thinking about a sound is at the mind-door, and comes after the hearing, which was at the ear-door.

Bāhiya. A discourse11 in the Udāna (the Inspired Utterances) tells of a man called Bāhiya, who wore clothes of bark and was honoured as a holy man, until a deva (heavenly being12) who had been his friend in a former life told him that he was not enlightened13 at all, and sent him to the Buddha. Bāhiya hurried to Sāvatthī, found the Buddha on his alms14 round, and begged him for a teaching there in the street. The Buddha told him:

“In that case, Bāhiya, you should train like this: ‘In the seen will be merely the seen; in the heard will be merely the heard; in the thought will be merely the thought; in the known will be merely the known.’ That’s how you should train.”

And he ended: “Just this is the end of suffering15.” Bāhiya understood at once, and became an arahant (fully enlightened) standing there. “In the seen, merely the seen” is this lesson in six words: seeing and colour, and no one who sees.

The Abhidhamma for Young Readers  ·  15

Page 15
Abhidhamma The Abhidhamma for Young (p. 1–20) p. 16

Never alone. No type of nāma (mind) or rūpa (matter) can occur by itself. They “can only exist in conjunction with other types of nama and rupa”. Seeing needs an eye and a colour; a moment of consciousness arises16 with mental factors17.

Three kinds of nāma. Nāma (mind) is divided into three kinds. Two are conditioned18: they arise because of causes. The third is unconditioned19. So the four paramattha dhamma (absolute realities) are:

the four paramattha dhamma (absolute realities)

citta cetasika rūpa nibbāna consciousness mental factors matter the end of all troubles the chief its helpers knows nothing unconditioned

conditioned: arise because of causes, and fall away unconditioned nāma: the first two · rūpa: the third no cause, no beginning, no end “The first three of these four realities are called conditioned.”

1. citta (consciousness) 2. cetasika (mental factors, or mental formations) 3. rūpa (matter) 4. nibbāna (the end of all troubles) The first three are conditioned. Nibbāna (the end of all troubles) is the one unconditioned reality.

What nibbāna is not. Nibbāna (the end of all troubles) “is not matter, it is not a place where one goes, it has no form or shape or solidity20, it is not something that one unites with”. It is a mental phenomenon, but different from consciousness and mental factors. It is unconditioned: “there are no causes which make it arise. It does not begin and it does not end. It does not experience anything, but it can be the object of experience.” It is experienced by lokuttara citta (consciousness beyond the world), the consciousness with fully developed wisdom. And it “cannot be understood intellectually21. It can only be directly experienced when wisdom has been sufficiently developed.”

Everything else is conditioned. All the other kinds of nāma (mind) and rūpa (matter) “arise because of past and present causes. They are all conditioned by one another.” A moment of seeing arises because there is an eye, a colour, light, attention and the result22 of a past deed23; it falls away24 at once; another moment follows.

Two truths. The ancient teachers spoke of two kinds of truth. Sammuti sacca (conventional25 truth) is the truth of everyday talk: there is a girl, she is sitting, she sees a flower. That is true in the way that “chariot26” is true. Paramattha sacca (ultimate27 truth) is the truth of what is really there: moments of citta (consciousness) with their cetasika (mental factors), and rūpa (matter). The Abhidhamma speaks only the second kind. The Suttas (the discourses) often speak the first, because the Buddha spoke to people in the way they could understand. The two do not contradict each other.

In seeing, the citta (consciousness) is the one that sees the object5. “Citta is the chief experiencer.” Everything else in the moment, the cetasika (mental factors6), helps the citta (consciousness) in its own way. The first two kinds are causes: they are kamma (deeds14) in the making, and will bring results in the future. The third kind is the result of causes in the past. The fourth kind is neither cause nor result.

Kusala citta: the good moments. Of the twenty-one kinds of kusala citta (good consciousness), eight belong to ordinary daily life. The book says they are divided “according to whether it is accompanied by pleasant or indifferent15 feeling, with wisdom or without wisdom and prompted16 or unprompted”. So a good moment may be glad or calm; it may understand or not understand; it may arise17 by itself or after some urging. The other thirteen are nine kinds of consciousness of the jhāna (deep calm of mind) and four kinds that experience nibbāna (the end of all troubles).

The book’s examples of good moments: “moments of generosity18 toward other beings19, moments of restraint20 from lying, killing or stealing, moments of respect for wise people, moments of insight21 into the true nature of things or moments of meditative22 absorption practising tranquility23 meditation”. Giving a mango to a friend; holding back from a lie; bowing to a teacher: each is kusala citta (good consciousness).

Akusala citta: the bad moments. There are twelve kinds of akusala citta (bad consciousness). Eight are rooted in lobha (attachment24), and these “are accompanied by pleasant or indifferent feeling”: wanting something can feel nice, or feel like nothing much. Two are rooted in dosa (anger), and these “are accompanied by unpleasant feeling”. Two are rooted in moha (ignorance25) alone, “accompanied by indifferent feeling, one with doubt and one with restlessness26“.

The book’s examples: “when we get angry, when we are bored, when we are depressed, when we are absorbed in beautiful things, when we kill or steal or lie to people or when we are restless”. Boredom is on the list, and so is being absorbed in beautiful things.

Vipāka citta: the results. The thirty-six kinds of vipāka citta (result consciousness) are “the result of previous skillful or unskillful deeds”. The book says: “When we see, hear, taste, smell or touch pleasant or unpleasant objects it is result.” Seeing a beautiful colour is the result of a good deed in the past. Hearing a harsh sound is the result of a bad deed in the past. The seeing and the hearing themselves are not good or bad; they are results.

Kiriya citta: neither cause nor result. The twenty kinds of kiriya citta (functional consciousness) “have no effect in terms of cause and result”. The book says they “occur in the sense-door and in thought processes27 of enlightened28 beings and again in 9 of the meditative states”. When a sound strikes the ear, the first citta (consciousness) to turn towards it is a kiriya citta (functional consciousness): it only turns to the object, it does not like or dislike. And when an arahant (fully enlightened person) smiles or gives or teaches, those moments are kiriya (functional) and not kusala (good), because an arahant (fully enlightened person) makes no more kamma (deeds).
